 The Gold Derby Q&A How Jasmine Burke found her way to ‘Beyond the Gates’ and a Daytime Emmy nomination
 The Atlanta native is thrilled to be part of a groundbreaking soap opera. By Ronda Racha Penrice October 30, 2026 11:00 am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jasmine Burke and Arielle Prepetit on Beyond the Gates Quantrell Colbert/CBS Share

 1 
 Jasmine Burke didn’t have awards expectations when she signed up to be part of the CBS soap Beyond the Gates . No one did. As the second soap to feature a Black cast since Generations debuted in 1989 (and ended in 1991), the first to be designed completely around a Black family, and the first new daytime soap to launch on a major broadcast network since 1999's Passions , the odds really didn’t spell out success. 
 Flash-forward almost two years and Beyond the Gates hasn’t just become a staple of CBS's daytime lineup, it’s also garnered a whopping 15 Daytime Emmys nominations. And one of those nods — Outstanding Guest Performance in a Daytime Drama Series — has Burke’s name on it for her role as June. 
 Related Stories ‘The Kelly Clarkson Show’ wins 4 Daytime Emmys, including Best Talk Show — but Sherri Shepherd stages an upset as Best Host 2026 Daytime Emmys: Complete list of winners includes Tamara Tunie, Kelly Clarkson, Star Jones (updating) 
 Beyond the Gates isn’t the first trailblazing project she’s been part of. The Atlanta native has also been a background singer for artists like CeeLo Green and appeared on MTV's Making the Band competition series. Acting, however, is what she really treasures.
 Gold Derby spoke with Burke who confessed that she never knows when she’ll appear on Beyond the Gates . "I just receive scripts out the blue," she shared. "I'm not a contract player, so I could receive a script or I could not. The fact that they've continued to write me in, I'm just grateful every time I receive that email."
 Gold Derby: Take us back to your thoughts and experiences at the very beginning of this journey with Beyond the Gates . 
 When I first read about Beyond the Gates years ago, I said, “That’s going to be a hit; people are really starving out here for diverse stories in daytime.” For it to go into production means that all of the people at CBS feel the same way. It’s such a historic network in its own right; they greenlit the first Black variety show with Clifton Davis and Melba Moore … so it made sense that they wanted to bring a Black soap opera to the world for this new generation.
 Your first IMDb credit was on reality TV, for Making the Band . How did you make the transition to acting? 
 Making the Band started with the boy groups, and that was considered a respectable way to have your singing talent seen and heard. It wasn’t considered reality television; you could get a real record deal, and you could really sell records around the world. I knew I could sing and dance, and the film and television industry hadn’t landed in Atlanta yet. I was like, “OK, I’ll take this chance and have my singing heard on national television, and that will lead to success in the entertainment business.” It didn’t lead to success for me in entertainment, but it is a badge of honor that I had a chance to be a finalist on the biggest talent competition in the world at the time.
 Burke as June on 'Beyond the Gates' Quantrell Colbert/CBS 
 I'm sure you were told "Oh, you have to go to New York or L.A. You can't do it from Atlanta." 
 Yes, I was told that so many times. I always thought that was a bizarre thing for people to say because nobody in L.A. is from L.A. They moved to L.A. from Kansas City, Oklahoma, Chicago, and Florida. I still had this deep sense that God gave me a talent, and he was going to make sure it reached the world some way, somehow. I just believed that strongly.
 And with my life circumstances at the time, I couldn’t just pick up and move to L.A., so I had to make it work in Atlanta. I made do with local theater, and then, when the tax credit came and Tyler Perry put up his first studio here, I was able to get work there. Slowly but surely, work started to trickle in. The networks started hearing that there was this little actress in Atlanta named Jasmine Burke, and they should probably call her if they wanted to get the job done. I built a reputation as a big fish in a small pond, and then the big fish started making the pond bigger.
 Beyond the Gates received 15 Daytime Emmy nominations, and you got a nomination! Where were you when you heard this news? 
 First, that's never happened — a soap opera receiving 15 nominations in its first year. We keep making history! I was off that day, and was in my robe when I received the call that I had been nominated. I didn't even know when it was being announced; this is my first time ever being submitted, so I didn't know what the process is. So when I received the call, I was literally frozen for an hour. I fell to my knees, and I was on the floor for like an hour, just in happy disbelief. It's too good to be true.
 How did you land the role of June on Beyond the Gates ? 
 Sheila Ducksworth, our visionary leader [and executive producer], had all these stories in her heart. June is a very pivotal role and they knew that they had to have a special actor to be able to bring her to life and tell this story. Over a decade ago, I starred on another series called Saints & Sinners , a nighttime soap. That was my first time being in a lead role on a television series. I thought no one had seen it, because the show was canceled, even though we were very successful. But Sheila told me recently that the reason why they offered me the role of June was because she saw my work on Saints & Sinners , so when this character of June came up, they knew they wanted a very powerful, strong actress, and she called me for the role.
 A scene from 'Beyond the Gate' Quantrell Colbert/CBS 
 How do fans react to June? 
 When I meet the fans, they see themselves [in her], and they see their aunts and their cousins. The response that I get a lot is that the story of an unhoused person is being told with so much dignity, and the fans really respect how much integrity that I've given June. I've made her human and relatable, and they appreciate being able to see that type of realness. But then it's also heartwarming and touching at the same time. People really feel seen and heard about June.
 What are the pivotal moments of June’s journey that stand out to you from this year? 
 The moment when she was with her sister Regina [Jacinte Blankenship], and her memory is coming back to her after literally blocking her life out of her mind because of the pain. It's so strange, as I'm talking to you, I see the parallel between my life and June's life. June didn't hold on to her past out of shame for the things that she felt; she put that guilt on herself that she didn't deserve anything good in life, and then she started receiving the help that got her life back on track and got her back in her children's lives. So that stands out to me and brings me to tears right now.
 A big part of playing June is thatit's helped me tap into: "Maybe Jasmine deserves that joyful expectation for herself." That's the incredible thing about this character — she's so real. I believe that's why people have connected with her so much; if we could just give ourselves permission to have that joy and to feel we are deserving how much better our lives can be! She has that effect on people and on me.
 Another moment is when she gets her dress and gets to have her Cinderella moment. She finally feels like, "OK, I can do this. Like I can live a good life, and I can be a part of my children's lives." That was very fulfilling. After all the hell she had been through, that Cinderella moment at the cotillion was beautiful.
